literary_identity: poet; satirist; orator regius; tutor to Prince Henry
biography: Educated at Cambridge and Oxford, where he was laureated (1488), and at Louvain (1492); he styled himself 'poet laureate'. Tutor to Prince Henry (the future Henry VIII) from about 1496 to 1502, he became rector of Diss in Norfolk (c. 1504) and 'orator regius' at court. His later career was a running satirical war with Cardinal Wolsey, whom he attacked in verse so freely that he took sanctuary at Westminster in 1523, where he died on 21 June 1529.
literary_profile: The dominant English poet of the early Tudor period and the inventor of the 'Skeltonic' line — short, breathless, rhymed couplets of irregular length. His canon runs from the dream-satire The Bowge of Courte (c. 1499) through the mock-elegy Philip Sparrow (c. 1505), the low-life tour de force The Tunning of Elinour Rumming (c. 1517), the morality play Magnificence (c. 1515–23), and the great anti-Wolsey satires Speke Parrot (1521), Colin Clout (c. 1522), and Why Come Ye Nat to Courte? (c. 1522–23), to the self-crowning dream vision The Garland of Laurel (1523).
stylistic_characteristics: The Skeltonic: tumbling short lines, obsessive rhyme, macaronic Latin, colloquial diction, and a satirical voice that moves between learned allusion and street abuse; also a master of the aureate, 'laureate' high style.
intellectual_concerns: The corruption of the clergy and the court; the duties of kingship; the poet's laureate authority; the defence of the English language against Latinate pretension.
historical_significance: The first great English satirist of the print era and the bridge between the medieval and Renaissance poetries; his Skeltonics were imitated for a century and admired by the Elizabethans, who read him as the scourge of Wolsey.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace uncertain; some Skeltonic attributions among minor poems remain debated.

literary_identity: humanist; lawyer; statesman; Lord Chancellor; martyr and saint
biography: Born in Milk Street, London, on 7 February 1478, the son of a judge; page to Cardinal Morton; studied at Oxford and the Inns of Court. A friend of Erasmus from 1499, he translated Lucian with him, wrote the Latin epigrams, and published Utopia at Louvain in 1516. Entered royal service in 1517; undersheriff of London, speaker of the Commons (1523), chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and Lord Chancellor (1529–32). Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was imprisoned in the Tower in April 1534 and beheaded on 6 July 1535; canonized in 1935.
literary_profile: The presiding genius of English humanism. Utopia (1516) invented the fictional commonwealth; The History of King Richard III (c. 1513–18), written in both Latin and English, is the first great work of English historical prose and the source of Shakespeare's Richard III; the controversial dialogues of 1529–33 (A Dialogue Concerning Heresies, The Supplication of Souls, The Confutation of Tyndale's Answer) are the summit of Reformation polemic; and A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation (1534), written in the Tower, is a masterpiece of devotional prose.
stylistic_characteristics: Irony, wit, and the dramatic management of dialogue; the plain English style of the later controversial works; Latinity of European standard in the epigrams and Utopia.
intellectual_concerns: The reform of Christendom and the commonwealth; the claims of conscience against the state; property, enclosure, and social justice; the defence of the old church against the new theology.
historical_significance: Author of the founding text of utopian fiction, the first classic of English historiography, and one of the great prose styles of the language; his life and death made him the exemplary conscience of the English Reformation.
biographical_uncertainty: None significant; the dating of Richard III's composition remains approximate.

biography: Born in Gloucestershire about 1494; educated at Oxford (BA 1512, MA 1515) and Cambridge. Denied episcopal patronage for an English Bible, he left England in 1524 and worked in Germany and the Low Countries: his New Testament was printed at Worms in 1526 and smuggled into England; the Pentateuch followed in 1530 and a revised New Testament in 1534. Betrayed at Antwerp in 1535, he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde on 6 October 1536.
literary_profile: The father of the English Bible. His translations — made from the Greek of Erasmus and the Hebrew — gave English scripture its enduring shape: the Authorized Version of 1611 retains perhaps ninety per cent of his New Testament phrasing. As a polemicist he wrote the most effective Reformation tracts in English: The Obedience of a Christian Man (1528), The Parable of the Wicked Mammon (1528), The Practice of Prelates (1530), and An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue (1531).
stylistic_characteristics: The plain style at its greatest: short sentences, monosyllabic Saxon diction, and rhythms tuned for reading aloud; learned argument made colloquial and urgent.
intellectual_concerns: The authority of scripture over church and prince; justification by faith; the translation of the Word into every ploughboy's language; the duty of obedience and its limits.
historical_significance: The principal architect of English biblical prose and of the language of English devotion; his translation work shaped the King James Bible and, through it, the speech of the English-speaking world.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his early Gloucestershire life rest on Foxe's Acts and Monuments.

biography: Born at Allington Castle, Kent, in 1503; educated at St John's College, Cambridge. A courtier and diplomat for Henry VIII — he was esquire of the body, ambassador in France, Italy, and Spain, and knighted in 1535 — he was twice imprisoned in the Tower: in 1536, during the fall of Anne Boleyn, and in 1541 on charges of treasonable correspondence. Released through the influence of Catherine Howard, he died of fever at Sherborne, Dorset, on 11 October 1542. His poems circulated in manuscript during his life; 96 were printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
literary_profile: The founder of the English lyric tradition. He introduced the Petrarchan sonnet into English (translating and imitating the Rime sparse with rugged, deliberate roughness), wrote the great courtly lyrics ('They flee from me', 'Whoso list to hunt', 'My galley charged with forgetfulness'), the three verse epistles known as the Satires (c. 1536), and a paraphrase of the seven penitential psalms composed after his 1536 imprisonment.
stylistic_characteristics: A difficult, compressed, colloquial style — enjambment against the rhyme, metrical irregularity used for dramatic emphasis, and the plain speech of the courtier set against Petrarchan convention.
intellectual_concerns: The dangers of court life under an absolute prince; the claims of truth against flattery; love, honour, and the unstable self; the psalmist's repentance as a model for the Tudor subject.
historical_significance: With Surrey, he established the sonnet, the courtly lyric, and the verse satire in English, providing the formal foundations of the Elizabethan poetic achievement; Tottel's printing of his verse made him the first modern English poet of the anthologies.
biographical_uncertainty: The canon rests on manuscript attributions (principally the Egerton MS); the extent of his relationship with Anne Boleyn is conjectural.

biography: Born at Hunsdon about 1516, eldest son of the Duke of Norfolk; brought up with the Duke of Richmond (Henry VIII's illegitimate son) and educated in the humanist manner. A soldier and courtier — he served in the French wars of the 1540s and was wounded at the siege of Montreuil — he was arrested in December 1546 on largely fabricated charges of quartering the royal arms, and beheaded on Tower Hill on 19 January 1547, the last victim of Henry VIII's reign. His poems circulated in manuscript and were printed in Tottel's Miscellany (1557); his translation of Aeneid II and IV was published in 1554 and 1557.
literary_profile: The refiner of the English sonnet: he gave the form the rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg) that became the 'English' or Shakespearean sonnet, and his smooth decasyllabic line pointed the way to the Elizabethan style. His translation of Virgil's Aeneid, Books II and IV — the first English blank verse — created the unrhymed iambic pentameter that Marlowe and Shakespeare made the language of English drama.
stylistic_characteristics: Regular, musical decasyllables; elegant management of the Petrarchan materials; a grave, chivalric sensibility; in the Aeneid translation, a new plainness of diction answering Virgil's.
intellectual_concerns: Nobility and honour under tyranny; love, constancy, and the ruin of Troy as an image of English court politics; the translation of classical epic into English verse.
historical_significance: Inventor (with Wyatt) of the English sonnet form and of blank verse — the two technical foundations of Elizabethan poetry and drama; his life and death dramatized the fate of the old nobility under the Tudors.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth year given as 1516 or 1517 in the records; some lyrics attributed to him in Tottel are of uncertain authorship.

literary_identity: archbishop of Canterbury; liturgist; theologian; martyr
biography: Born at Aslockton on 2 July 1489; fellow of Jesus College, Cambridge. His suggestion that the universities should judge the validity of Henry VIII's marriage brought him to the king's notice; he became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1533 and presided over the annulment, the royal supremacy, and the dissolution. Under Edward VI he produced the two Books of Common Prayer (1549, 1552), the Book of Homilies (1547), and the Forty-Two Articles (1553). Under Mary he was tried, degraded, and — after recanting and then withdrawing his recantations — burned at Oxford on 21 March 1556, thrusting the hand that had signed the recantations first into the fire.
literary_profile: The architect of the English liturgy. The Book of Common Prayer is his monument: collects, services, and the prose of worship that fixed the devotional language of English for four centuries ('ashes to ashes, dust to dust'). He was the principal author of the first Book of Homilies (1547) and of the doctrinal statement of the Edwardian church.
stylistic_characteristics: Ritual prose of unmatched gravity and compression: parallel phrasing, scriptural cadence, and the direct address of congregation by priest; a style built for the voice.
intellectual_concerns: Worship in the vernacular; the simplification of the liturgy on scriptural principles; royal supremacy and the reform of doctrine; the unity of the English church.
historical_significance: Author of the defining text of Anglican worship, still in daily use; the Prayer Book's prose ranks with Tyndale's Bible as the foundation of modern English devotional language.
biographical_uncertainty: None significant; the division of authorship within the 1547 Homilies is partly editorial.

biography: Born of a yeoman family at Thurcaston about 1485; educated at Cambridge, where he was converted from conservative orthodoxy to the reformed faith in the 1520s. A preacher of extraordinary popular power, he became bishop of Worcester in 1535, resigned in 1539 over the Six Articles, and preached through the Edwardian years, notably the Sermon of the Plough (1548) and the Lent sermons before Edward VI (1549). Under Mary he was imprisoned with Ridley and Cranmer and burned at Oxford on 16 October 1555, urging Ridley: 'we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.'
literary_profile: The greatest English preacher of the Reformation. His printed sermons — above all the Sermon of the Plough and the Sermons before King Edward VI — are the classics of Tudor homiletics: plain, concrete, homely in metaphor, and fearless in their attack on landlords, enclosers, and corrupt clergy.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain style made dramatic: rural simile, proverb, anecdote, and direct address; a yeoman's concreteness yoked to scriptural authority.
intellectual_concerns: Preaching as the cure of the commonwealth; social justice against enclosure and greed; the duty of bishops and landlords; the Word before ceremony.
historical_significance: The model of English preaching for a century and a principal voice of the Reformation's social conscience; his sermons document the moral crisis of mid-Tudor England.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

literary_identity: playwright; polemicist; antiquary; bishop of Ossory
biography: Born at Cove, Suffolk, on 21 November 1495; entered the Carmelite order at Norwich, then converted to the Reformation in the 1530s. He wrote King Johan (c. 1538), the first English history play and a weapon of Henrician propaganda; The Image of Both Churches (c. 1545), a running commentary on Revelation; and the Illustrium Maioris Britanniae Scriptorum Summarium (1548), the first bio-bibliography of British writers. Bishop of Ossory in Ireland in 1553, he fled abroad under Mary and returned under Elizabeth, dying at Canterbury in November 1563.
literary_profile: The founder of English literary history and of the Protestant history play. King Johan turned the chronicle matter of England into stage polemic, and the Summarium — enlarged at Basel in 1557–59 as the Scriptorum Illustrium Maioris Brytanniae Catalogus — preserved the names and titles on which later literary history rests.
stylistic_characteristics: Furious polemical energy; the apocalyptic scheme of the two churches applied to history; catalogue and inventory as instruments of scholarship and propaganda alike.
intellectual_concerns: The identification of the pope with Antichrist; the English church and nation as God's elect; the record of British writers as proof of national dignity.
historical_significance: Inventor of the English history play and of English literary bibliography; his catalogues transmitted knowledge of the medieval English canon to the Renaissance.
biographical_uncertainty: None significant.

biography: Born about 1497, probably in London; a singer, musician, and entertainer at the court of Henry VIII and the household of Princess Mary. He married Joan Rastell, the niece of Thomas More, and remained a Catholic: in 1564 he left England for Mechelen, where he died about 1580. His interludes were played at court and in the great households, and his collections of proverbs and epigrams were bestsellers for a century.
literary_profile: The master of the Tudor interlude. The Four PP, The Play of the Weather, and A Play of Love turn the debate form into comedy of ideas — the palmer, pardoner, pothecary, and pedlar disputing who can tell the greatest lie; Jupiter taking petitions on the weather. His A Dialogue Conteynyng the Nomber in Effect of All the Prouerbes in the Englishe Tongue (1546) collected the proverb wisdom of England, and The Spider and the Fly (1556) is the great allegorical poem of the Marian reaction.
stylistic_characteristics: Deadpan comic logic, punning debate, and the proverb as structural unit; a style that teaches while it jokes, and jokes while it teaches.
intellectual_concerns: The comedy of opinion and authority; religious satire from within orthodoxy; the wisdom of proverb lore; the politics of the Reformation seen from the losing side.
historical_significance: The first English comic dramatist of the print era and the conduit by which the interlude became the comedy of the Elizabethan stage; his proverb collections fixed the common sayings of the language.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the dating of the interludes is largely inferential.

biography: Born about 1490 into a family of west-country lawyers; he served Wolsey as clerk and became a diplomat and clerk of the king's council. Falling from favour in the 1530s, he devoted himself to letters: The Boke Named the Governour (1531), dedicated to Henry VIII, The Castle of Health (1534), and the first Latin–English dictionary (1538). He died on 26 March 1546.
literary_profile: The principal English theorist of humanist education and the gentleman magistrate. The Governour — drawing on Castiglione, Erasmus, and the Italian humanists — defined the curriculum, the virtues, and the physical training of the ruling class, and it introduced scores of classical commonplaces into English prose. His Dictionary (1538) founded English lexicography.
stylistic_characteristics: Earnest, copious Ciceronian prose; the deliberate enrichment of English vocabulary from Latin; a moralist's directness beneath the classical apparatus.
intellectual_concerns: The education of princes and magistrates; the union of learning and virtue in the ruling class; the health of body and commonwealth; the capacities of the English language.
historical_significance: Author of the classic statement of the Tudor educational ideal, read by every Elizabethan schoolmaster, and of the dictionary that began the English lexicographical tradition.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

literary_identity: humanist; tutor to Elizabeth I; Latin secretary
biography: Born at Kirby Wiske about 1515; educated at St John's College, Cambridge, where he taught Greek and reformed the pronunciation of it. Tutor to Princess Elizabeth from 1548 to 1550, he served as Latin secretary under Mary and Elizabeth. His Toxophilus (1545), a dialogue in praise of archery, won him a royal pension, and The Schoolmaster, begun about 1563, was published posthumously in 1570 by his widow. He died on 30 December 1568.
literary_profile: The most readable of the English humanist educators. Toxophilus is the first English treatise on a sport and a model of the plain style; The Schoolmaster — built around the instruction of the young Elizabeth — attacks Italianate corruption, prescribes the double translation of Latin, and records the educational practice of the age in the finest English prose between More and Hooker.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain style refined into art: concrete, anecdotal, sinewy English that he explicitly opposed to the inkhorn inflation of his contemporaries.
intellectual_concerns: The education of the English governing class; the discipline of imitation and translation; the morality of travel; archery and bodily training as parts of the curriculum.
historical_significance: Tutor and intellectual model of Elizabeth I; The Schoolmaster governed English pedagogical theory for two centuries and remains the classic defence of the vernacular for learning.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth year approximate (1514 or 1515).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English (writing in England); Scottish by birth
biography: Born about 1484, probably in Scotland; educated perhaps at Oxford, he became a priest, chaplain at the college of St Mary Ottery in Devon, then a Benedictine monk of Ely and finally rector of All Hallows, Lombard Street. He died at Croydon in June 1552. His Ship of Fools (1509) adapted Sebastian Brant's Narrenschiff through Locher's Latin, and his five Eclogues (c. 1514) introduced pastoral to England.
literary_profile: The first English pastoralist and the translator of the most widely read satire of the age. The Ship of Fools is a comprehensive estates satire — a gallery of fools from the scholar to the bishop — written in fluent rhyme royal and five-line stanzas, and the Eclogues, based on Mantuan, moralize the shepherd's life and the corruption of courts and clergy.
stylistic_characteristics: Smooth, competent stanzaic verse; moral satire without Skeltonic fury; a translator's fidelity to his Latin sources over originality.
intellectual_concerns: The folly of the estates; clerical reform; the moral uses of pastoral; the dignity of English as a literary language.
historical_significance: Introduced both the estates satire of the continental Renaissance and the pastoral eclogue into English; a principal channel by which humanist satire reached the Tudor reading public.
biographical_uncertainty: Birthplace and early life uncertain; the date of the Eclogues is approximate.

biography: Born about 1474, probably in Suffolk; educated perhaps at Oxford, he became groom of the chamber to Henry VII. His Pastime of Pleasure was printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1509 and The Example of Virtue about 1504; he died about 1523, the last significant poet of the Chaucerian-Lydgatian school.
literary_profile: The last of the medieval allegorists and a favourite of the early Tudor court. The Pastime of Pleasure recounts the education, courtship, and knightly career of the hero Graunde Amoure in rhyme royal and couplets, an allegorical summa of chivalric and learned ideals; The Example of Virtue traces the soul's progress through Youth to Age and Eternity.
stylistic_characteristics: Aureate diction in the Lydgatian manner; rhyme royal handled with fluency; allegorical machinery of pilgrimage, tower, and tournament.
intellectual_concerns: The seven liberal arts; chivalric education and courtly love; the soul's moral progress; the poet's role as teacher of princes.
historical_significance: The bridge between the medieval allegorical tradition and Tudor court poetry; Spenser read him, and The Pastime of Pleasure kept the dream-allegory alive into the Renaissance.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; little is known of his life beyond his court service.

biography: Born in London about 1503; educated at St Paul's School under William Lily and at Cambridge, Oxford, and Paris. Commissioned in 1533 as King's Antiquary, he travelled England and Wales in the 1530s and 1540s recording libraries, monuments, and topography, planning a vast description of Britain he never completed. He went mad in the late 1540s and died on 18 April 1552. His Itinerary remained in manuscript until the eighteenth century.
literary_profile: The father of English antiquarianism. His Itinerary notes preserve the record of monastic libraries on the eve of the Dissolution and remain a primary source for English topography; his Cygnea Cantio (1545), a Latin poem on the Thames, and his other Latin verse earned him a European reputation in his lifetime.
stylistic_characteristics: The note-taking style of the field antiquary: inventories, measurements, and reports jotted on the road, without literary finish.
intellectual_concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the description of the realm; the preservation of manuscripts and monuments against the destruction of the Dissolution.
historical_significance: Founded the study of British antiquities and preserved irreplaceable evidence of medieval England; his collections were quarried by every later antiquary from Bale to Camden.
biographical_uncertainty: None significant; the Itinerary's exact itinerary chronology is editorial.

biography: A London draper, alderman, and sheriff (1493–94), Fabyan retired from civic life about 1502 and compiled his chronicle of England and France, which he finished by 1504 (with continuations to 1509). He died in London in 1513, and the work was printed by Richard Pynson in 1516 as The New Chronicles of England and France.
literary_profile: Author of the standard London chronicle of the early Tudor period. Organized annalistically around the mayors and sheriffs of London, Fabyan's chronicle supplied Shakespeare and the Tudor historians with the matter of English history from Brutus to Henry VII, and its verse interjections ('L'envoy') give it a distinctly civic literary character.
stylistic_characteristics: The annalist's plain record, organized by civic year; occasional moralizing verse; a Londoner's eye for pageant, execution, and civic ceremony.
intellectual_concerns: The history of England and France as moral example; the dignity and record of the city of London.
historical_significance: The principal vernacular chronicle between the Brut tradition and Hall; a chief source of Tudor historical consciousness and of Shakespeare's history plays at second hand.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date unknown.

biography: Born in London about 1497; educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, and at Gray's Inn. A lawyer and MP, he compiled his great chronicle of the Wars of the Roses, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York, which Richard Grafton printed in 1548, the year after Hall's death.
literary_profile: Author of the chronicle that made the Tudor interpretation of history — the Wars of the Roses as God's judgement on rebellion, culminating in the providential union under the Tudors — the official story of England. Shakespeare drew the material of his English history plays, often nearly phrase by phrase, from Hall's Union through Holinshed.
stylistic_characteristics: Ample, oratorical prose; set speeches composed for the great men of the action; the providential scheme applied to the narrative of faction and battle.
intellectual_concerns: The horror of civil war; the legitimacy and providence of the Tudor dynasty; history as the school of princes.
historical_significance: The principal historiographical source of Shakespeare's histories and of the Elizabethan understanding of the fifteenth century; his set speeches shaped the English historical imagination.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

biography: Born at Southampton in 1504; educated at Winchester and Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Headmaster of Eton from 1534 (dismissed in 1541) and later of Westminster, he was a reformer who prospered under Edward VI and Mary alike. His Ralph Roister Doister, written about 1552, was printed about 1566. He died on 23 December 1556.
literary_profile: Author of the first English comedy. Ralph Roister Doister — five acts of Roman comedy built on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus, with the braggart soldier, the parasitic Merrygreek, and the London widow Dame Christian Custance — transplanted classical comic structure into English life and English verse, establishing the pattern the Elizabethan comedians followed.
stylistic_characteristics: Doggerel couplets of deliberate comic roughness; the miles gloriosus and the cunning servant in English dress; songs and jigs built into the action.
intellectual_concerns: The imitation of Roman comedy; school drama as moral and rhetorical training; the comic punishment of vanity and presumption.
historical_significance: Wrote the first English comedy on the classical model, the direct ancestor of the Elizabethan stage comedy; his school drama linked the interlude tradition to the professional theatre.
biographical_uncertainty: The precise date and first printing of Roister Doister are uncertain (c. 1552–53, printed c. 1566).

biography: Born about 1462; educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, and employed as chaplain and notary to Cardinal John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury. His Fulgens and Lucrece, played at Morton's household at Lambeth about 1497, is the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell about 1512–16. He died about 1502.
literary_profile: Author of the first secular English drama. Fulgens and Lucrece dramatizes a humanist debate — whether nobility lies in birth or in virtue — as a Roman comedy of courtship, complete with a subplot in which two servants, A and B, compete for the audience's employment; his Nature is a full-scale morality play of man's fall and amendment. Both were played in Morton's great hall, the seedbed of the Tudor interlude.
stylistic_characteristics: Debate framed as drama; the interweaving of serious argument and servant comedy; the morality convention put to secular and humanist use.
intellectual_concerns: True nobility and the claims of virtue over birth; the reform of manners; the education of the great household through play.
historical_significance: Bridging medieval morality and humanist comedy, Fulgens and Lucrece begins the secular English stage tradition that runs to the Elizabethan theatre.
major_influences: the humanist debate (Buonaccorso's De Vera Nobilitate)
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.

biography: Born about 1488 in the North Riding of Yorkshire; educated at Cambridge and an Augustinian friar before converting to the Reformation. Working in Antwerp, he produced the first complete printed English Bible in 1535, and he edited the Great Bible of 1539, which was ordered to be read in every parish church. Bishop of Exeter in 1551, he went into exile under Mary and returned under Elizabeth, dying on 20 January 1569.
literary_profile: The translator of the first complete printed English Bible. The Coverdale Bible (1535), translating chiefly from German and Latin versions, gave the English church its Psalter — still sung as Coverdale's version in the Book of Common Prayer — and the Great Bible (1539) put an English Bible in every parish church, its wording (largely Tyndale's) forming the base of the Authorized Version.
stylistic_characteristics: A flowing, musical prose less angular than Tyndale's; mastery of the cadence of the Psalms; the dignity of liturgical English.
intellectual_concerns: The complete vernacular Bible; the Psalter in English worship; the reform of the church through the Word.
historical_significance: Completed the English Bible and fixed the English Psalter; the Coverdale Psalms remain in liturgical use into the twenty-first century.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth year approximate; the exact place of printing of the 1535 Bible (Antwerp or Cologne) is debated.

biography: Born about 1496; a lawyer of Lincoln's Inn who married Margaret, Thomas More's eldest daughter, in 1521, and lived in More's household at Chelsea for sixteen years. He wrote The Life of Sir Thomas More between about 1553 and 1558 from intimate memory; it circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1626. He died on 4 January 1578.
literary_profile: Author of the first great English biography of a private man. The Life of Sir Thomas More — the portrait of the Chancellor at Chelsea: his prayers, his jests, his relations with his family, and his final refusal of the oath — is the classic of Tudor life-writing and the foundation of the More legend that Shakespeare's play and the later tradition inherited.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, affectionate, anecdotal prose; the vivid recalled dialogue of the Chelsea household; a son-in-law's reverence without hagiographical inflation.
intellectual_concerns: The memory and example of More; conscience against the state; the sanctity of the family and the household.
historical_significance: Established the English biographical tradition and supplied the human More to every later age; a primary source of the first importance for the English Reformation.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

literary_identity: bishop of Rochester; theologian; cardinal; martyr and saint
biography: Born at Beverley in 1469; educated at Cambridge, where he became Master of Michaelhouse and chancellor of the university, and the patron of Erasmus and of Greek studies. Bishop of Rochester from 1504, he was the confessor of Lady Margaret Beaufort and the most respected preacher of his age. Refusing the oath of supremacy, he was made a cardinal by Paul III and executed on 22 June 1535; canonized in 1935.
literary_profile: The great conservative preacher of the early Reformation. His sermons — against Luther (1521) and on the penitential psalms — are the classic statements of the old orthodoxy in the new age of print, and his commentary on the seven penitential psalms (1505, enlarged 1508) was the devotional bestseller of the early Tudor period.
stylistic_characteristics: Scholastic learning in a plain, forceful pulpit style; the expository sermon built on the literal text; pastoral warmth under doctrinal rigour.
intellectual_concerns: The defence of the old faith; penance and the sacrament; the reform of the clergy from within; the university as the church's school.
historical_significance: The intellectual leader of English Catholicism in the crisis of the 1520s and 1530s; his life and death defined the conservative alternative to the Henrician settlement.
biographical_uncertainty: None significant.

biography: Born about 1515; a scholar of Oxford who became corrector of the king's printing under Edward VI and a prolific editor and compiler. His Treatise of Moral Philosophy appeared in 1547; his prose satire Beware the Cat, written in 1552–53, was printed in 1561. He planned and partly compiled A Mirror for Magistrates, printed in 1559 after his death. He died about 1563.
literary_profile: The author of the first English work of sustained prose fiction and the begetter of A Mirror for Magistrates. Beware the Cat — a night-long exchange of stories about cats, set in a London printing house and framed as a fantastic listening experiment — is the first English novel in embryo, and its anti-Catholic satire made it dangerous enough to be suppressed. The Mirror, which he edited and contributed to, became one of the most influential books of the Elizabethan age.
stylistic_characteristics: Framed narrative in the plain style; printer's-shop realism; satirical fable with a serious theological edge.
intellectual_concerns: Protestant polemic against the old religion; the uses of fiction for truth-telling; the moral instruction of magistrates through the falls of great men.
historical_significance: A founding figure of English prose fiction and of the complaint tradition; his Mirror for Magistrates supplied subjects and rhetoric to Spenser, Shakespeare, and the whole Elizabethan tragic imagination.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the division of authorship within the Mirror is editorial.

biography: Born about 1521 into a Lincolnshire gentry family; married against her will to Thomas Kyme. Her refusal to accept the doctrine of transubstantiation brought her before the authorities in 1545 and 1546; racked in the Tower — reportedly by the Lord Chancellor himself — she was burned at Smithfield on 16 July 1546. Her accounts of her two examinations were printed with John Bale's commentary in 1546–47.
literary_profile: Author of the first English autobiography of a Protestant martyr and the most important woman's voice of the Henrician Reformation. The Examinations record her interrogations in her own words — scriptural, witty, and unyielding — and made her the exemplary female witness of the English church, read and reprinted through the sixteenth century and canonized by Foxe.
stylistic_characteristics: First-person testimony in the plain style; scriptural riposte reported as dialogue; a cool exactness under the shadow of the stake.
intellectual_concerns: The right of the laity, and of women, to read and interpret scripture; the sacrament debated as doctrine; the witness of the body against the bishops.
historical_significance: The founding text of English women's religious autobiography and a landmark of the martyrological tradition; her voice resounds in Foxe and in the later women writers of the Reformation.
major_influences: the Lollard tradition of lay testimony
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of the racking rest on Foxe and Bale.

biography: Born about 1512; the sixth wife of Henry VIII, whom she married in 1543. A learned woman of reformist sympathies, she narrowly escaped arrest for heresy in 1546. Her Prayers or Meditations appeared in 1545, the first book printed under the name of an English queen, and The Lamentation of a Sinner in 1547 after the king's death. She died on 5 September 1548, shortly after marrying Thomas Seymour.
literary_profile: The first English queen in print. Prayers or Meditations (1545) adapts the Imitatio Christi into a personal devotional idiom, and The Lamentation of a Sinner (1547) is a conversion narrative and confession in the new evangelical mode, declaring the futility of works and the sufficiency of faith in Christ.
stylistic_characteristics: Warm, first-person devotion; the language of interiority and the afflicted conscience; scriptural quotation woven into prayer.
intellectual_concerns: Personal faith and justification; the education of women (she oversaw the schooling of the young Elizabeth); the reform of devotion from within the court.
historical_significance: A pioneer of English women's devotional writing and a patron of the reformed cause; her example licensed the religious authorship of later English women.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth year approximate (1512); the extent of her direct influence on Elizabeth's education is documented but partly inferential.

literary_identity: grammarian; first High Master of St Paul's School
biography: Born at Odiham about 1468; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek. Appointed by John Colet as the first High Master of St Paul's School in 1512, he wrote the Latin grammar that, revised by Colet and Erasmus, became the standard school grammar of England. He died in February 1522 (new style 1523).
literary_profile: Author of the grammar that schooled England for three centuries. The Short Introduction of Grammar ('Lily's Grammar'), with its English accidence and its Latin Brevissima Institutio, was prescribed by royal proclamation under Henry VIII and Edward VI and memorized by every grammar-school boy from Shakespeare to Johnson — who quotes it, and its misquotations, throughout the literature of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The schoolmaster's clarity: paradigms, rules in English for boys, Latin examples; a grammar written to be memorized.
intellectual_concerns: The reform of Latin teaching on humanist principles; the founding of a public grammar school; the union of Greek learning with Christian education.
historical_significance: The author of the most widely used textbook in English history; Lily's Grammar structured the linguistic formation of the entire literate class of early modern England.
biographical_uncertainty: The exact division of the grammar's authorship among Lily, Colet, and Erasmus is editorial.

literary_identity: humanist; dean of St Paul's; founder of St Paul's School
biography: Born in London in 1467, son of a Lord Mayor; studied at Oxford and in Italy. His Oxford lectures on the epistles of St Paul (c. 1497–1505) broke with scholastic method and made him the father of English humanism; he became dean of St Paul's in 1505 and founded St Paul's School in 1509, appointing William Lily its first master. He died on 16 September 1519. His grammatical treatise, the Aeditio, was printed in 1527.
literary_profile: The founder of the Oxford reform that produced English humanism. His Paul's lectures, teaching scripture from the plain text rather than the glosses, converted a generation — including Erasmus, who called him the ideal of the Christian humanist — and his Aeditio contributed the English accidence to the standard school grammar.
stylistic_characteristics: Expository clarity aimed at the unlearned; plain-text biblical exposition; the reformer's impatience with ceremonial and gloss.
intellectual_concerns: The primitive church as model; education as the reform of Christendom; the layman's access to scripture.
historical_significance: The inspirer of Erasmus and More and the founder of the English humanist movement; his school and his lectures set the intellectual course of the Tudor century.
biographical_uncertainty: None significant; the Aeditio's precise date of composition is approximate.

literary_identity: physician; humanist; founder of the Royal College of Physicians
biography: Born about 1460, probably at Canterbury; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek from Politian and took a medical degree at Padua. Physician to Henry VIII, tutor of the young Thomas More, and founder of the Royal College of Physicians (1518), he translated Galen into Latin with unprecedented accuracy and wrote De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis (1524), the first scientific Latin grammar by an Englishman. He died on 20 October 1524.
literary_profile: The English pioneer of Greek medicine and philology. His Galen translations (1517–23) restored the texts of ancient medicine to the West, and his Latin grammar, applying the new philology to the classical language, is a landmark of English humanism.
stylistic_characteristics: The philologist's precision; translation as recovery of the original; grammar as science rather than schoolroom drill.
intellectual_concerns: The restoration of Greek learning; the reform of medicine on Galenic foundations; the accurate use of Latin among physicians and scholars.
historical_significance: Founded the scientific study of medicine in England and the College of Physicians; his translations and grammar made him, with Colet and Grocyn, one of the three pillars of the Oxford reform.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate.

biography: Born in London about 1475; a lawyer of the Middle Temple and the brother-in-law of Thomas More, whose circle he printed. His press issued More's early works and his own plays — The Four Elements (c. 1520) and the translation Calisto and Melebea (c. 1530) — and his chronicle The Pastime of People (c. 1529). His opposition to the clergy's exactions brought him imprisonment, and he died in prison in June or July 1536.
literary_profile: The first English printer-playwright. The Four Elements is a didactic interlude teaching cosmology and geography through drama, and The Pastime of People compresses the history of Britain into a popular chronicle; his press was the vehicle of the More circle and of the earliest English humanist drama.
stylistic_characteristics: Instruction through entertainment; the interlude as lecture hall and theatre at once; plain prose and functional verse.
intellectual_concerns: Popular education in the new learning; the reform of clerical exactions; law, printing, and the spread of knowledge.
historical_significance: A founder of the English printing trade in its humanist phase; his interludes and chronicles made the new learning available to a popular audience.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the date of his death (1536) is established by legal records.

literary_identity: biographer; gentleman usher to Cardinal Wolsey
biography: Born in Suffolk about 1497; entered the service of Cardinal Wolsey as gentleman usher about 1522 and attended him through his fall and death in 1530. Retiring to Suffolk, he wrote The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey between about 1554 and 1558 from his intimate knowledge of the Cardinal's household. The work circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1641. He died about 1562.
literary_profile: Author, with Roper's Life of More, of the twin masterpiece of Tudor biography. The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey — the rise, magnificence, and fall of the butcher's son who ruled England — is the classic of Tudor life-writing: eyewitness, circumstantial, and tragic, with the great scenes (Wolsey's fall at Cawood, his death at Leicester) rendered as drama. Shakespeare drew on it for Henry VIII.
stylistic_characteristics: Ample, plain narrative prose; the usher's exact memory for gesture, word, and scene; tragic structure imposed on recent history.
intellectual_concerns: The fall of princes as moral example; the memory of Wolsey against his detractors; loyalty to the great house he had served.
historical_significance: With Roper, founded English secular biography; his portrait of Wolsey — and through it of Henry VIII's court — shaped the English historical imagination from Shakespeare onward.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.

biography: Born about 1490 in Sussex; educated at Oxford and a Carthusian monk before leaving the order to practise medicine. He travelled widely in Europe and the Mediterranean, and his books — The Dyetary of Health (1542) and The First Book of the Introduction of Knowledge (1547) — made him the first English writer of popular medicine and travel. He died in the Fleet prison in April 1549.
literary_profile: The first English popular medical writer and the father of the English travel book. The Dyetary prescribes diet and regimen in plain English for the common reader, and The Introduction of Knowledge — the first English book of travels written from personal observation — describes the peoples of Europe in prose and verse, with specimens of their languages.
stylistic_characteristics: Homely, practical prose; the physician's plain advice; travellers' tales told with a journalist's eye for the odd and useful.
intellectual_concerns: Popular health and regimen; the description of foreign nations; the usefulness of knowledge to the commonwealth.
historical_significance: Founded the English traditions of popular medicine and of the travel book; his writings document the widening world of the Tudor reader.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; parts of the biography rest on late testimony.

literary_identity: playwright; composer; master of the choristers at St Paul's
biography: Born about 1486; almoner and master of the choristers at St Paul's Cathedral, where he trained the boys who performed his play Wit and Science (c. 1539). He was a noted composer and organist — John Heywood married his daughter — and died in 1547.
literary_profile: Author of Wit and Science, the most accomplished of the school moralities: the allegory of Wit's wooing of Lady Science, with the giant Tediousness, the Vice Idleness, and the comic conversion of the booby Ingnorance, written for boy actors with songs and dances. The play survives in a single manuscript with its music cues.
stylistic_characteristics: The morality convention refreshed with music, dance, and schoolroom comedy; allegorical personification handled with theatrical tact.
intellectual_concerns: The marriage of wit and learning; the discipline of the school; the education of boys through play and music.
historical_significance: The finest of the school interludes and a direct ancestor of the academic drama and the court masque; his St Paul's boys became one of the great Elizabethan playing companies.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the play's date (c. 1539) is editorial.

alternative_names: Sir David Lindsay of the Mount
literary_identity: poet; playwright; herald; Lyon King of Arms
biography: Born about 1486 at the Mount in Fife; attached to the court of James IV and the companion and usher of the young James V, whom he exhorted in The Dreme (1528). Lyon King of Arms from 1542 and a lord of session, he was the leading advocate of the reformed cause in Scottish letters. His Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis was played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552. He died about April 1555.
literary_profile: The major Scottish poet of the Reformation. The Dreme (1528) instructs the young king in a dream vision; The Testament of the Papyngo (1530) is a dying parrot's satire of court and clergy; and Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis — the great morality of the Scottish Reformation — stages the trial of the estates before King Humanitie, with John the Common-Weill the plaintiff and the vices of the church in the dock.
stylistic_characteristics: Direct satirical address in fluent Scots; the dream vision and the testament turned to political use; the morality play expanded to a national parliament.
intellectual_concerns: The reformation of the Scottish church; the education of the king; the common weal against the estates; justice for the poor.
historical_significance: The poet of the Scottish Reformation and the author of its greatest dramatic work; the Satyre is the summit of Scots drama and was played and reprinted for generations.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the exact date of his death (1555) is uncertain within the year.

biography: Born about 1474, third son of the Earl of Angus; educated at St Andrews and provost of St Giles, Edinburgh. His Palice of Honour (c. 1501) and the allegories King Hart and Conscience followed; his Eneados, the translation of Virgil's Aeneid completed on 22 July 1513, is the first complete rendering of the poem in any British language. Bishop of Dunkeld from 1515, he died in London of the plague in September 1522.
literary_profile: The last great poet of the Scottish Chaucerians and the first British translator of the Aeneid. The Palice of Honour is a courtly dream vision of dazzling learning; King Hart an allegory of the heart's court; and the Eneados — in vigorous Scots couplets, with a prologue to each book describing the Scottish seasons — ranks with Surrey's as one of the two great Tudor translations of Virgil.
stylistic_characteristics: Aureate Chaucerians diction in the allegories; in the Eneados, a plain, energetic Scots that renders Virgil's gravitas in northern idiom; the seasonal prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots.
intellectual_concerns: The translation of classical epic into the vernacular; honour, fame, and the education of princes; the defence of poetry against its detractors.
historical_significance: Author of the first complete Aeneid in any form of English and the summit of the Scottish Chaucerians; his Eneados passed the classical inheritance to the northern Renaissance.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the dating of King Hart is editorial.

biography: Born at Lichfield about 1480; studied at Oxford, where he was laureated for grammar. He taught in London and wrote a series of grammatical and rhetorical textbooks, of which the Vulgaria (1520) — model sentences in Latin and English for schoolboys — is the most famous. He died about 1553.
literary_profile: The most successful school grammarian of the generation before Lily's Grammar was standardized. The Vulgaria's paired Latin and English sentences, drawn from everyday school and city life, are at once a textbook and a vivid picture of early Tudor London, and its jibes at Lily made it a document of the grammar wars of the 1520s.
stylistic_characteristics: The schoolmaster's sentence-builder; colloquial English paired with schoolboy Latin; combative prefaces addressed to rival grammarians.
intellectual_concerns: The teaching of Latin through the vernacular; the rivalries of the grammar schools; the manners and language of London boys.
historical_significance: A principal maker of the Tudor school curriculum; the Vulgaria is a unique record of the spoken English of the early sixteenth century.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.
